# Why Add Covariates to a Group Comparison?

Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) is a linear regression containing categorical
group indicators and continuous or additional categorical covariates. It can
improve precision by explaining outcome variation known before treatment, adjust
an observational comparison for measured confounding under strong assumptions,
or describe how group differences vary across a covariate.

For group $G_i$ and covariate $X_i$, a basic model is

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_GG_i+\beta_X(X_i-x_0)+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{E}(\varepsilon_i\mid G_i,X_i)=0.
$$

If $G_i$ is binary and there is no $G_iX_i$ interaction, $\beta_G$ is the adjusted
mean difference at every value of $X$ represented by this model. Centering at
$x_0$ makes the intercept scientifically meaningful but does not change fitted
values or $\beta_G$. With multiple groups, the indicators are simply a
multi-degree-of-freedom regression term.

The estimand must precede the method. It might be a treatment effect at a common
baseline value, an average adjusted contrast over a target covariate distribution,
or a purely descriptive conditional association. The fitted coefficient is an
estimator; its realized value is an estimate. Adjustment alone does not determine
which interpretation is justified.

# Adjusted Means Are Model-based Predictions

Let the fitted model have coefficient vector $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$. An adjusted
mean for group $g$ at covariate value $x_0$ is

$$
\widehat m_g(x_0)=\mathbf x(g,x_0)^\mathsf{T}
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}.
$$

An adjusted contrast is therefore

$$
\widehat\Delta(x_0)
=\{\mathbf x(1,x_0)-\mathbf x(0,x_0)\}^\mathsf{T}
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}.
$$

Its estimated variance is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\{\widehat\Delta(x_0)\}
=\mathbf c(x_0)^\mathsf{T}
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})
\mathbf c(x_0).
$$

"Adjusted mean" is incomplete unless the analyst states where or how covariates
were averaged. Equal weighting across groups targets a different population from
weighting by the observed sample frequencies. Predictions at the grand mean of a
covariate may describe no actual unit when the distribution is multimodal or
when covariates interact.

# The Parallel-slopes Assumption

The model above assumes the same covariate slope in every group. A model allowing
effect modification is

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_GG_i+\beta_X(X_i-x_0)
+\beta_{GX}G_i(X_i-x_0)+\varepsilon_i.
$$

Now the adjusted group contrast at $X=x$ is

$$
\Delta(x)=\beta_G+\beta_{GX}(x-x_0).
$$

Thus $\beta_G$ is only the contrast at the centering value. If an interaction is
present, deleting it to recover a single ANCOVA p-value answers the wrong
question. Show conditional contrasts or predictions over the region with support,
and define any average contrast with explicit target-population weights.

Linearity in $X$ is also an assumption, not a property of covariance adjustment.
Transformations or splines can model curvature while retaining regression-based
group contrasts. Categorizing a continuous covariate usually discards information,
creates artificial thresholds, and leaves residual confounding.

# Regression-based ANOVA and Nested Models

ANOVA, ANCOVA, and ordinary regression use the same least-squares machinery.
Suppose a reduced model has design matrix $\mathbf X_R$ and a full model adds
$q$ estimable columns, producing residual sums of squares $RSS_R$ and $RSS_F$.
Under the classical Gaussian linear model,

$$
F=rac{(RSS_R-RSS_F)/q}{RSS_F/(n-p_F)}
\sim F_{q,n-p_F}quad\text{under the reduced-model null}.
$$

The test asks whether the added coefficients are jointly zero conditional on all
terms retained in both models. This formulation makes the hypothesis explicit:

- adding all group indicators tests an adjusted group effect;
- adding group-by-covariate terms tests whether slopes differ;
- adding a block or batch factor tests that term conditional on the specified
  biological design;
- adding nonlinear basis terms tests the chosen departure from linearity.

Models compared by this partial $F$ test must be fitted to the same observations.
If missingness changes the analysis set, a difference in residual sum of squares
mixes model change with data change. Robust or cluster-aware Wald tests may be
preferable when the classical variance assumptions fail.

# Baseline Adjustment in Randomized Studies

In a randomized two-arm study with baseline measurement $Y_0$ and follow-up
$Y_1$, a common model is

$$
Y_{1i}=\beta_0+\beta_TT_i+\beta_BY_{0i}+\varepsilon_i.
$$

Because treatment is randomized, chance baseline imbalance does not confound the
treatment effect. Adjusting for a prognostic baseline value generally improves
precision and targets the follow-up mean difference conditional on the prespecified
model. It is commonly more efficient than analyzing change
$Y_1-Y_0$, which implicitly fixes the baseline coefficient at one and can amplify
measurement error.

Baseline must be measured before assignment or treatment. Adjusting for a
post-treatment variable can remove part of the effect, induce collider bias, or
change the estimand. In observational studies, pre-exposure covariates may address
measured confounding only if the adjustment set, functional forms, positivity,
measurement, and missingness assumptions are defensible. More covariates are not
automatically safer.

# Imbalance, Coding, and Sums of Squares

With balanced orthogonal designs, sequential and partial decompositions coincide.
With imbalance, a reported "adjusted effect" depends on the other terms in the
model and on the contrast being tested. A useful workflow is:

1. draw the design and identify experimental units, randomization, blocks, and
   measured covariates;
2. define the target contrast and target covariate distribution;
3. encode the full mean structure, including prespecified interactions and
   nonlinearities;
4. verify rank, overlap, and estimability;
5. express the hypothesis as a coefficient contrast or reduced-versus-full model;
6. report predicted means and contrasts with uncertainty.

Software "Type I," "Type II," or "Type III" labels cannot replace steps 2 and
5. In particular, a main-effect test in the presence of interaction may average
over factor levels using weights unrelated to the target population. Empty or
sparse factor-by-covariate regions can turn adjusted comparisons into extrapolation.

# Assumptions and Diagnostics

ANCOVA inherits the linear-model assumptions and adds special risks around
covariate choice and overlap.

| Assumption or risk | Consequence | Diagnostic or sensitivity analysis |
|---|---|---|
| Independent experimental units | Pseudoreplication understates uncertainty | Map sampling and assignment; use cluster-aware or multilevel analysis |
| Correct conditional mean | Adjusted contrasts can be biased or target a projection | Plot residual and partial relationships; compare justified interactions and smooths |
| Common slope when interaction is omitted | One number masks changing contrasts | Fit and display prespecified group-by-covariate interactions |
| Covariate overlap across groups | Adjustment otherwise extrapolates | Plot distributions and joint support; restrict the target population if needed |
| Valid covariate timing and role | Post-treatment or collider adjustment can bias causal claims | Use design chronology and a causal diagram; report alternative justified sets |
| Valid variance and dependence model | Standard errors and tests can be miscalibrated | Inspect heteroskedasticity and clustering; use appropriate robust covariance or models |
| Reliable covariate measurement | Error leaves residual confounding and can alter slopes | Use validation data or measurement-error sensitivity analysis |

Residual diagnostics cannot prove that the adjustment set controls confounding.
Conversely, a chance correlation between treatment and baseline in a randomized
sample is not evidence that randomization failed. Design knowledge supplies
assumptions that the observed data alone cannot verify.

# Worked Bioinformatics Example

Suppose 48 patient-derived organoid lines are randomized to control or drug, and
log-expression of a pathway at 24 hours is the outcome. Prespecified covariates
are baseline pathway expression, tissue of origin, and sequencing batch.

The organoid donor line is the experimental unit. Replicate wells, libraries,
and reads nested within one line are technical replication. If wells receive
treatment independently but share a donor, the model must still represent donor
clustering and the precise assignment scheme.

An ANCOVA contrast estimates the adjusted drug-control difference at specified
baseline and tissue values, or averaged over a declared tissue and baseline
distribution. A drug-by-baseline interaction would make that difference vary
with baseline expression. Batch adjustment can improve precision when treatment
is represented within batches; if treatment and batch are perfectly confounded,
no regression can identify their separate effects.

Statistically, an interval quantifies uncertainty about the adjusted contrast
under the model and design. Biologically, a nonzero contrast supports a treatment-
associated change in this pathway for the sampled donor population and assay; it
does not alone prove pathway mediation, clinical relevance, or transferability
to patients.

# Reporting and Connections

Report the estimand, experimental unit, design, covariate timing and selection,
model formula, coding and centering, overlap, adjusted means and contrasts with
their weighting scheme, intervals, joint tests, diagnostics, missing-data handling,
and sensitivity to interactions, nonlinearities, influential units, and
alternative justified adjustment sets.

- [One-way and factorial ANOVA](one-way-and-factorial-anova.qmd) introduces
  designed group comparisons, factorial interactions, and omnibus tests.
- [Multiple linear regression](multiple-linear-regression.qmd) supplies the
  conditional-mean and partial-regression foundation.
- [Categorical predictors and contrasts](categorical-predictors-and-contrasts.qmd)
  explains coding, estimability, and marginal-mean weights.
- [Interaction terms and effect modification](interaction-terms-and-effect-modification.qmd)
  develops conditional contrasts and scale dependence.
- [Linear-model assumptions and diagnostics](linear-model-assumptions-and-diagnostics.qmd)
  separates mean, variance, dependence, and causal assumptions.
- [Regression uncertainty and coefficient interpretation](regression-uncertainty-and-coefficient-interpretation.qmd)
  derives uncertainty for linear combinations and predictions.

1. ANCOVA is multiple regression with group indicators and covariates; adjusted
   means are model-based predictions.
2. Define where or over whom a contrast is averaged before interpreting it.
3. A common adjusted group effect requires an adequate parallel-slopes model;
   interaction makes the contrast covariate-dependent.
4. Baseline adjustment in randomized studies can improve precision, but
   post-treatment adjustment can change or bias the target effect.
5. Regression cannot repair absent overlap, treatment-batch confounding, or
   technical pseudoreplication.
